L10-a4f633: **Anticholinergic medications** (antimuscarinics) are a cornerstone of urologic pharmacotherapy, primarily for **overactive bladder (OAB)** and **neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD)**.<sup>[[1]](#ref1)[[2]](#ref2)</sup> They block muscarinic receptors (M2 and M3) in the detrusor muscle, inhibiting involuntary contractions, increasing bladder capacity, and reducing urgency and frequency.
L12-415a39: The class has six FDA-approved agents with broadly similar efficacy but meaningfully different tolerability, CNS penetration, and dementia-risk profiles. The 2022 SUFU White Paper on anticholinergics and dementia risk and the 2024 AUA/SUFU OAB guideline together have shifted contemporary practice toward β3-agonist-first positioning for many OAB patients, with anticholinergics reserved for specific indications, combination therapy, or patient-specific factors.

L186-cccd2b: **EAU 2026 (non-neurogenic female LUTS)** offers anticholinergics to women with OAB who fail conservative management (Strong) and advises shared decision-making, extended-release formulations whenever possible, early review of efficacy and adverse effects, and, if a drug fails, dose escalation, a different formulation or a β3 agonist alone or combined (all Strong). Immediate-release products allow flexible or on-demand dosing but cause more adverse events. EAU finds no anticholinergic clearly superior for cure or improvement and reports that most patients stop within three months. For older women it advises caution with long-term use, especially with existing or risk of cognitive dysfunction, and assessment of anticholinergic burden (Strong). Cognitive harm is cumulative with exposure (level 2); oxybutynin may worsen cognition, while darifenacin, fesoterodine, solifenacin and trospium have not been shown to in short-term studies (level 1b).<sup>[[31]](#ref31)</sup>
